scan_strategy: Stripe (initial melt), and remelting strategies: same direction (SD), reverse direction (RD), 67° rotation (67°RT), 90° rotation (90°RT), and chess (5×5 mm²)
scan_strategy_evidence: To investigate the effect of various remelting strategies on cracking, the following approaches were employed (see Fig. 1 ): remelting the solidified layer using stripe scanning strategy in (1) the same direction (SD) and (2) reverse direction (RD) with respect to the initial melt layer. Remelting was performed at a (3) 67° (67°RT) and (4) 90° (90°RT) rotational angle relative to the initial melt layer. (5) The 5 × 5 mm² chess scanning strategy was employed for remelting
shielding_gas_evidence: The IN939 powders were produced via argon gas atomization
optimal_parameters: Single remelting under chess strategy with laser power 125 W, scanning speed 1250 mm/s, hatch spacing 60 μm, layer thickness 30 μm (for initial melt)
optimal_parameters_evidence: Compared to the initial melt sample (laser power: 125 W, scanning speed: 1000 mm/s), employing single remelting under the chess strategy, with laser power set at 125 W and scanning speed at 1250 mm/s, led to a substantial 85% reduction in crack density (from 0.13 mm/mm² to 0.02 mm/mm²) and a notable 60% decrease in porosity (from 0.15% to 0.06%) in IN939.
crack_type: Solidification cracking and solid-state cracking (including ductility dip cracking and strain-age cracking)
crack_type_evidence: Solidification cracking occurs when insufficient feeding of residual liquid between the dendrites cannot accommodate the solidification shrinkage at the end of solidification, which tends to feature a structure with cellular and dendrite arms. Solid-state cracking happens when the grain boundary sliding induced by γ' precipitation or thermal stress is hindered at the grain boundary precipitates or triple junctions and stress concentrations are formed. It differs from solidification cracking in the morphology. The solid-state cracks are mostly straight and distributed along grain boundaries, and can be further categorized into ductility dip cracking (DDC) and strain-age cracking (SAC).
crack_location: Along grain boundaries and within cellular dendrite structures
crack_location_evidence: The solid-state cracks are mostly straight and distributed along grain boundaries. Solidification cracking occurs when insufficient feeding of residual liquid between the dendrites cannot accommodate the solidification shrinkage at the end of solidification, which tends to feature a structure with cellular and dendrite arms.
crack_cause: Residual stresses from high cooling rates and repeated thermal cycles, and insufficient feeding of residual liquid between dendrites during solidification shrinkage
crack_cause_evidence: The high cooling rates and repeated thermal cycles inherent in L-PBF introduce substantial residual stresses in fabricated samples, leading to the formation of hot and solid-state cracking. Solidification cracking occurs when insufficient feeding of residual liquid between the dendrites cannot accommodate the solidification shrinkage at the end of solidification.
sensor_methods_used: Optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with backscattering electron detector, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with STEM and EDS, X-ray diffraction (XRD), EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction)
sensor_methods_evidence: Sequential polishing with polishing paste from 3.5 μm to 1.5 μm was performed. To ensure the representativeness of crack and porosity statistics, images of the samples were collected using an Axio Image A2m type optical microscope at 50 × magnification. The microstructure, crack morphology, and element distribution were examined on longitudinal (XZ-) and transversal (XY-) sections of the L-PBF-processed IN939 samples, which were parallel and vertical to the building direction, respectively. This examination was carried out using a ZEISS Sigma 500 field emission scanning electron microscope (FEM-SEM) equipped with a backscattering electron detector (BSD). A Tecnai G2 F30 transmission electron microscope equipped with a scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) and an X-ray energy spectrometer (EDS) system was employed for nano-scale phase characterization and compositional analysis at 300 kV. The structural analysis of the fabricated IN939 was performed using a D8 ADVANCE X-ray diffractometer in reflection mode.

crack_cause_evidence: Solidification cracking in nickel-based superalloys primarily stems from two factors: shrinkage pores between dendrites in the late stages of solidification and high-melting-point carbides. As the melt pool remains in a solid-liquid coexistent state, γ-cells and grains nucleate extensively and grow into dendrites. During this stage, solute elements in the alloy continuously segregate into the interdendritic liquid, precipitating hard and brittle carbides that gradually form liquid films as solidification progresses.
